message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I did the right thing or not in this situation. Let me start by understanding what happened. A few years ago, I was renting a place with this dude, and we were on a lease. When the lease was ending, he just left without giving much notice. He took most of his stuff, but left a few things and a note saying he didn't want to bring those things with him. Now, where I live, if you don't get rid of your stuff when you move out, the landlord can pay someone to remove it, and that cost comes out of your deposit. I've heard of people losing $250 just because someone had to take three milk crates of their stuff to the dump. That's a rip-off. So, I tried to contact him for two weeks, texting and emailing, asking him to pick up his stuff or let me take them to the dump. But he never responded. I ended up taking most of his stuff to the dump, but he had around 60 video games for the PS4. I thought, why not sell them? There's a local game store that buys used games, and they gave me $600 for all of his games. Fast forward to last week, I saw him at a party, and we were being polite. He asked how the move-out was, and I said it was good. Then he asked what I did with his stuff. When he found out I sold his games, he got mad. I told him I tried to get him to grab those things, but he never reached out. Now he's calling me an asshole and asking me to pay him back. I checked, and legally, there's nothing I did wrong. But now I'm wondering if I'm the asshole for doing this. Okay, so to figure this out, I need to think about the different aspects of the situation. First, the lease agreement. Did the lease specify what happens to belongings left behind? If it doesn't, then legally, the landlord can dispose of them as they see fit, which usually means charging the tenant for removal costs. In this case, the landlord didn't dispose of the games; instead, you took the initiative to sell them. Legally, since the games were left behind and the landlord didn't claim them, you might have a case for ownership. But morally, is it right to sell someone else's belongings without their consent? Also, consider the effort you put in to contact him. You tried for two weeks, which shows you made an effort to give him a chance to retrieve his stuff. But he didn't respond, so you took action to prevent him from losing money on his deposit. On the other hand, selling his games for $600 is a significant amount. He might feel that you profited from his belongings without his permission, which could make him upset. Another angle is the relationship aspect. You saw him at a party, and he's now calling you an asshole. This could affect your relationship, even if legally you're in the right. Maybe there's a way to make amends or explain your actions better to him. Also, think about the value of the games. If they're worth $600, maybe you could offer him a portion of that money as a goodwill gesture. It might help ease the tension and show that you're willing to compromise. In summary, while you might not be legally in the wrong, the moral and relational aspects are more complex. It's important to balance doing what's right legally with maintaining good relationships and showing empathy towards others' feelings.
